course.title: SQL Masterclass
course.tagline: Zero to advanced, one module at a time.
course.standard: PostgreSQL-first, with MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server notes.
course.description: Module 09 teaches safe UPDATE and DELETE: assignments, expressions, subqueries, UPDATE FROM, DELETE USING, RETURNING and the difference from TRUNCATE.
outcomes: Update one or many rows safely
Use expressions and CASE in SET

modules.title: UPDATE, DELETE and Data Modification
modules.goal: Modify and remove rows safely, with verification and rollback.

topics.title: What Is UPDATE?
topics.simple: UPDATE existing rows ke values badalta hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE is DML that changes column values for rows matched by an optional WHERE clause and returns a count of affected rows.
points: Without WHERE it targets every row.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: UPDATE Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition.
topics.pro: The syntax is UPDATE table SET column = expression [, ...] [FROM ...] [WHERE ...] [RETURNING ...].
points: SET lists assignments separated by commas.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S' WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating One Column
topics.simple: Ek column ki value badalne ke liye ek assignment likho.
topics.pro: A single-column UPDATE assigns one expression to one column for every matched row.
points: Use the primary key in WHERE for a single row.
The new value must satisfy the column type.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns ko comma se update karo.
topics.pro: Multiple assignments run in one statement; all expressions see the row values from before the statement, not the just-assigned values.
points: Assignments are evaluated from the old row.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S', marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating Specific Rows
topics.simple: WHERE se sirf intended rows update karo.
topics.pro: A WHERE predicate targets specific rows; a unique key gives the smallest and safest target.
points: Match on a key when possible.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 88 WHERE id = 2;

topics.title: UPDATE with WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE ke bina UPDATE poore table ko chhu sakta hai.
topics.pro: WHERE filters the target rows before assignment; omitting it updates every row in the table.
points: Use IS NULL for null checks.
Test the predicate with SELECT first.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 0 WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with Expressions
topics.simple: New value purani value par calculation ho sakti hai.
topics.pro: The SET expression can reference existing columns, arithmetic, functions and CASE, and is evaluated for each matched row.
points: The result must fit the column type.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with CASE and COALESCE
topics.simple: CASE conditional value deta hai; COALESCE fallback deta hai.
topics.pro: CASE chooses a value per row, while COALESCE replaces NULL with a fallback; both are common in data-repair updates.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET email = COALESCE(email, 'unknown@example.com');

topics.title: UPDATE with Subquery
topics.simple: Subquery se naya value compute kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery in SET must return at most one row and one column; a multi-row result raises an error.
points: A NULL subquery result assigns NULL.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with FROM
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me UPDATE FROM doosri table se values laata hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE ... FROM joins the target to a source relation; each target row should match at most one source row to keep the result deterministic.
points: Duplicate source matches make the update unpredictable.

example.sql: UPDATE students s SET marks = a.marks FROM applicants a WHERE s.email = a.email;

topics.title: RETURNING with UPDATE
topics.simple: RETURNING updated rows wapas deta hai.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns the new row values for every updated row, including generated values and expressions.
points: It can return old values only via a CTE or trigger.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: What Is DELETE?
topics.simple: DELETE rows ko table se hataata hai.
topics.pro: DELETE is DML that removes rows matched by WHERE and returns the number deleted.
points: Without WHERE it removes every row.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 3;

topics.title: DELETE Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition.
topics.pro: The syntax is DELETE FROM table [USING ...] [WHERE ...] [RETURNING ...].

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60;

topics.title: DELETE Specific Rows
topics.simple: WHERE se specific row delete karo.
topics.pro: A precise predicate deletes only the intended rows; a primary key is the safest target.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 4;

topics.title: DELETE with Conditions
topics.simple: Range, list aur NULL conditions delete me bhi kaam karte hain.
topics.pro: DELETE accepts the same boolean predicates as SELECT, including comparisons, IN, LIKE and IS NULL.
points: Use IS NULL for null checks.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: DELETE with Subquery
topics.simple: Subquery se decide kar sakte hain kaunse rows delete honge.
topics.pro: DELETE with IN or EXISTS uses a subquery to choose rows; beware NOT IN with NULLs, which can match nothing.
points: IN works for a list of keys.
NOT EXISTS is safer with NULLs.
The subquery must be correct before deleting.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

topics.title: DELETE with USING
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me DELETE USING doosri table se join karke rows delete karta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE ... USING adds source relations to the WHERE join, removing target rows that match the source.
points: Join the target and source in WHERE.
A row is deleted at most once.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students s USING enrollments e WHERE s.id = e.student_id AND e.course_id = 10;

topics.title: RETURNING with DELETE
topics.simple: RETURNING deleted rows ko wapas deta hai — archive ke liye useful.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns the deleted row values, which can be inserted into an archive table in the same statement.
points: Return the rows before they disappear.
Combine with a CTE to archive.
RETURNING does not prevent the delete.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE
topics.simple: DELETE filtered aur trigger-friendly hai; TRUNCATE poora table jaldi khali karta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE removes selected rows, fires row triggers and is transactional; TRUNCATE removes all rows, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and is transactional in PostgreSQL.
points: TRUNCATE resets storage; RESTART IDENTITY resets sequences.

example.sql: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

topics.title: Safe Modification Practices and Common Errors
topics.simple: Bade UPDATE/DELETE se pehle SELECT, transaction aur row count check karo.
topics.pro: Safe modification means previewing the target rows, wrapping the change in a transaction, checking the affected count and using RETURNING or a backup before committing.
points: Commit only after the count matches.
Use RETURNING for an audit trail.

learn.q: What does UPDATE do?
learn.why: UPDATE is DML that changes column values.

learn.q: What does DELETE do?
learn.why: DELETE is DML that removes rows.

learn.q: What happens to UPDATE without WHERE?
options: Only the first row is updated
learn.why: Without a predicate, UPDATE targets the whole table.

learn.q: What happens to DELETE without WHERE?
options: Only the first row is deleted
learn.why: Without a predicate, DELETE removes all rows.

learn.q: Which clause limits UPDATE or DELETE?
learn.why: WHERE selects the target rows.

learn.q: How do you update two columns at once?
learn.why: SET name = ..., marks = ... updates both.

learn.q: What does RETURNING do?
learn.why: RETURNING exposes changed or deleted rows.

learn.q: Which value does SET marks = marks + 5 use?
learn.why: Assignments read the row as it was before the statement.

learn.q: Which function supplies a fallback for NULL?
learn.why: COALESCE returns the first non-null argument.

learn.q: What must a scalar subquery in SET return?
options: At most one row and one column
learn.answer: At most one row and one column
learn.why: A scalar subquery must produce a single value.

learn.q: Which PostgreSQL clause joins a source table to UPDATE?
learn.why: UPDATE ... FROM adds source relations.

learn.q: Which PostgreSQL clause joins a source table to DELETE?
learn.why: DELETE ... USING adds source relations.

learn.q: Does DELETE keep the table structure?
learn.why: DELETE removes rows; the table remains.

learn.q: Does TRUNCATE support WHERE?
learn.why: TRUNCATE always targets the whole table.

learn.q: Does DELETE fire row-level DELETE triggers?
learn.why: DELETE removes rows individually and fires row triggers.

learn.q: Does TRUNCATE fire row-level DELETE triggers?
learn.why: TRUNCATE does not delete rows one by one.

learn.q: Does DELETE reset an identity sequence?
learn.why: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY resets it.

learn.q: Can DELETE be rolled back in PostgreSQL?
learn.why: DELETE is transactional.

learn.q: What does UPDATE ... RETURNING show?
options: The old row values by default
learn.why: RETURNING returns the updated row as stored.

learn.q: What is the safest target for UPDATE?
learn.why: A unique key targets exactly the intended row.

interview.q: What is UPDATE?
interview.answer: DML that changes column values for rows matched by WHERE and returns the affected count.

interview.q: What is DELETE?
interview.answer: DML that removes rows matched by WHERE and returns the deleted count.

interview.q: What happens without WHERE in UPDATE or DELETE?
interview.answer: The statement targets every row in the table.

interview.q: How do multiple SET assignments evaluate?
interview.answer: All expressions read the row values from before the statement, not values assigned earlier in the same SET list.

interview.q: How do you update from another table in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Use UPDATE ... FROM source WHERE join_condition; each target row should match at most one source row.

interview.q: How do you delete using another table in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Use DELETE FROM target USING source WHERE join_condition; each target row is deleted at most once.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: Returns the changed or deleted rows in the same statement.

interview.q: What is a scalar subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery that returns at most one row and one column, usable where a single value is expected.

interview.q: What happens if a SET subquery returns multiple rows?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL raises an error because the subquery is not scalar.

interview.q: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DELETE supports WHERE, fires row triggers and removes selected rows; TRUNCATE removes all rows, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and resets storage.

interview.q: Is TRUNCATE transactional in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Yes, it can be rolled back there; MySQL performs an implicit commit.

interview.q: Does DELETE reset identity?
interview.answer: No; use TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY or reset the sequence explicitly.

interview.q: How do you archive deleted rows?
interview.answer: Use DELETE ... RETURNING inside a CTE and insert the returned rows into an archive table.

interview.q: Why is DELETE with NOT IN and NULL dangerous?
interview.answer: The NULL comparison makes the predicate unknown, so no rows may be deleted; NOT EXISTS is safer.

interview.q: Why can a foreign key block DELETE?
interview.answer: Child rows still reference the parent and the constraint has no cascade action.

interview.q: What happens if UPDATE changes a primary key?
interview.answer: It can break foreign keys or fail on duplicates; use ON UPDATE CASCADE only when the relationship requires it.

interview.q: Why use a transaction around a large modification?
interview.answer: It lets you verify the affected count and roll back cleanly if the change is wrong.

interview.q: Why can a large UPDATE be expensive?
interview.answer: It creates new row versions, writes WAL, updates indexes and can bloat the table until vacuum runs.

interview.q: Why can a large DELETE be expensive?
interview.answer: It creates dead tuples, writes WAL and must maintain indexes; batching reduces lock time.

interview.q: What is the safest modification workflow?
interview.answer: Preview with SELECT, open a transaction, run the change with RETURNING, verify the count, then commit or roll back.

labs.title: Update one column
labs.task: Set marks to 95 for id 1.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Update two columns
labs.task: Set name and marks for id 1.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S', marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

labs.title: Update a specific row
labs.task: Set marks to 88 for id 2.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = 88 WHERE id = 2;

labs.title: Update with an expression
labs.task: Add five marks to every known mark.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;

labs.title: Update with CASE
labs.task: Raise every mark below 60 to 60.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = CASE WHEN marks < 60 THEN 60 ELSE marks END;

labs.title: Fill missing emails
labs.task: Replace NULL emails with unknown@example.com.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET email = COALESCE(email, 'unknown@example.com');

labs.title: Update from a subquery
labs.task: Set NULL marks to the average marks.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) WHERE marks IS NULL;

labs.title: Update from another table
labs.task: Copy marks from applicants by matching email.
labs.solution: UPDATE students s SET marks = a.marks FROM applicants a WHERE s.email = a.email;

labs.title: Update with RETURNING
labs.task: Update id 1 and return the new row.
labs.solution: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name, marks;

labs.title: Update with a transaction
labs.task: Update id 1 inside a transaction and commit.

labs.title: Delete one row
labs.task: Delete id 4.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 4;

labs.title: Delete with a condition
labs.task: Delete students below 60.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60;

labs.title: Delete by subquery
labs.task: Delete students enrolled in course 10.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

labs.title: Delete with USING
labs.task: Delete students enrolled in course 10 using a join.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students s USING enrollments e WHERE s.id = e.student_id AND e.course_id = 10;

labs.title: Delete with RETURNING
labs.task: Delete id 3 and return the row.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 3 RETURNING *;

labs.title: Archive deleted rows
labs.task: Delete marks below 60 and insert them into students_archive.
labs.solution: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) INSERT INTO students_archive SELECT * FROM deleted;

labs.title: Truncate the table
labs.task: Remove every row and reset identity.
labs.solution: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

labs.title: Safe update
labs.task: Preview, update, verify and commit in one transaction.

labs.title: Safe delete
labs.task: Delete id 5 inside a transaction and roll back.
labs.expected: The row is returned but the delete is undone.

labs.title: No-op delete
labs.task: Delete id 999 and observe the count.
labs.solution: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 999;

logic.q: Why is UPDATE without WHERE dangerous?
logic.answer: It changes every row in the table, often with one mistaken statement.

logic.q: Why is DELETE without WHERE dangerous?
logic.answer: It removes every row and leaves an empty table.
The SELECT shows exactly which rows the predicate matches before you modify them.

logic.q: Why wrap a modification in a transaction?
logic.answer: You can verify the affected count and roll back if the change is wrong.
It shows the changed rows and supports an audit or archive without a second query.

logic.q: Why does DELETE support WHERE but TRUNCATE does not?
logic.answer: DELETE removes selected rows one by one; TRUNCATE is a whole-table storage operation.

logic.q: Why does DELETE fire row triggers but TRUNCATE does not?
logic.answer: DELETE processes rows individually; TRUNCATE does not visit them as row deletes.

logic.q: Why is changing a primary key risky?
logic.answer: Foreign keys reference the old value; without ON UPDATE CASCADE the change can fail or orphan relationships.

logic.q: Why must a SET subquery be scalar?
logic.answer: A column assignment needs one value per row; multiple rows cannot fit.

logic.q: Why can UPDATE FROM be unpredictable with duplicate sources?
logic.answer: A target row matched by several source rows may be updated more than once with no defined winner.

logic.q: Why is NOT IN with a NULL subquery unsafe for DELETE?
logic.answer: The NULL comparison makes the predicate unknown, so it can delete nothing.

logic.q: Why can a foreign key block DELETE?
logic.answer: Referencing child rows still exist and the constraint has no cascade action.

logic.q: Why batch a very large DELETE?
logic.answer: Small batches reduce lock time, WAL spikes and blocking for other sessions.

logic.q: Why vacuum after many updates or deletes?
logic.answer: The old row versions become dead tuples; vacuum reclaims that space.

logic.q: Why does DELETE not reset identity?
logic.answer: The sequence is a separate object; only an explicit restart changes it.

debug.fix: UPDATE students SET marks = (SELECT marks FROM applicants LIMIT 1);

debug.fix: DELETE FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id IS NULL);

debug.fix: UPDATE students SET marks = 100 WHERE id = 1;

DELETE FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10;

debug.fix: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name;

revision.answer: Changes existing rows matched by WHERE.

revision.q: How do you update two columns?
How do you return changed rows?
How do you update from another table?
How do you delete using another table?

revision.answer: DELETE filters and fires row triggers; TRUNCATE removes all rows and keeps the table.
Preview, transact, modify, verify the count, then commit or roll back.
